scenes.title: Choose the report for the question
scenes.narration: Reports brings several questions together: who is currently staffed, what happened on calls, and which timestamps have been recorded. In our fictional Chicago Fire department, begin with the Reporting catalog. Find Staffing Report and use its View Report button. The report groups people by their latest recorded staffing level and provides a count and chart. Truck 81 has people in Available, Unavailable and On Shift categories. This is a staffing summary; it does not establish who physically attended an incident.

scenes.title: Define a Call Summary period
scenes.narration: On the Call Summary Report parameter page, check Report Start Time, Report End Time and Group before using Run Report. scenes.title: Understand how calls are assigned to groups
scenes.narration: Calls by Group explains why a call belongs to a reporting group. Each call counts once. A containing group geofence is used first; otherwise the report uses the group associated with most dispatched resources. Some calls can remain unassigned. This is different from simply listing the current viewer’s group. Here, Firehouse 51 has seven calls and Command has five. Use the explanation when investigating a surprising group total instead of changing memberships to make a report match expectations.

scenes.title: Set the Call Unit Times window
scenes.narration: Call Unit Times answers a more specific question: which dispatch and status timestamps exist for each unit on each call? Its parameter form has start and end times and Run Report. Here the range starts October twenty-fourth at twenty-three thirty and ends October twenty-ninth at twenty-three thirty. That begins thirty minutes earlier than our first Call Summary. Keep those periods distinct when reconciling the results.

scenes.title: Interpret timestamps and their linkage
scenes.narration: The generated report has Dispatched, En Route, On Scene, Staging, Cleared and Linked By columns. The original DEMO rows say Dispatch only and leave later status times blank. A dispatch entry alone does not establish an arrival. Other exercise rows say Unit status. Read the recorded timestamps as they stand; some are incomplete or out of order, so review the underlying history before calculating a duration. Some calls explicitly report no unit dispatch or status data. The native exercise shows Ambulance 61 with dispatch and en-route times, while its later cells remain blank. These are software records, not independent physical-arrival verification.

scenes.title: Download and interpret the real CSV
scenes.narration: Use Download CSV on this report to obtain its unit rows for the same parameters. The downloaded file includes call and unit identifiers, timestamps and Linked By. This exercise export contains thirteen unit rows for twelve distinct calls: a call with two units creates two rows, while a call with no unit rows contributes none. The file uses DispatchOnly and Explicit codes where the screen says Dispatch only and Unit status. Keep blank times blank, and retain the report period with your file.

scenes.title: Read yearly, quarterly and monthly tables
scenes.narration: The longer period also produces Yearly Statistics. An asterisk marks a partial period; the note explains that the report covers only part of it. Do not describe that row as a complete calendar year. Quarterly Statistics adds YTD, the cumulative call count within the report’s included periods for that year. Monthly Statistics uses the same Calls and YTD distinction. October contains five calls. November and December show zero calls while YTD remains five. These are results from available records in the chosen range, not forecasts of future activity.

scenes.title: Apply the same checks across departments
scenes.narration: Chicago Fire can review station call distribution; community care and mental-health teams can review operational workload without putting client histories into report notes. Search-and-rescue teams can compare mission-period groups. Security teams can inspect recorded staffing before a patrol review, while wildland coordinators can compare seasonal reporting windows. Industrial teams can examine unit status chronology during a software exercise. In each setting, choose the question, fix the period and scope, inspect the detail rows, and explain missing data before sharing an authorized result.
